correctness.rationale: CG residual orthogonality makes the normalized residual polynomial the degree-k orthogonal polynomial for the positive discrete spectral measure with masses b_i^2. Its roots are real Ritz values inside the active spectral interval. When kappa<=2, every factor 1-lambda/theta lies in [-1,1], so the residual polynomial is at most one in every active coordinate and x_i=x_i^*(1-p_k(lambda_i)) is nonnegative. Two dimensions terminate in at most two active modes. For every kappa>2, the three-mode epsilon family has a second residual polynomial converging to the two-point annihilator whose value at the high mode is kappa-1>1. The exact rational witness was replayed from the packaged verifier.

Their full text gives CG's Krylov characterization and finite termination in at most the number of active spectral modes.
The source does not claim that these iterates stay in a coordinate cone below any condition threshold.

Statement-level searches for CG positivity, Ritz-polynomial sign bounds, BFGS/Broyden nonnegative iterates, and diagonal sign loss found no implication-equivalent theorem. Nearby published numerical-optimization findings concern objective or Euclidean-norm behavior rather than orthant membership.
residual_risks: Older CG or orthogonal-polynomial literature may contain the same coordinatewise implication without using positivity or orthant terminology.
The root-location lemma is classical, so an unlocated source specializing it to diagonal nonnegative right-hand sides could make the theorem previously implicit.
The quasi-Newton corollary is not independently novel once the CG theorem and the published identical-iterate result are combined; its role is to show the scope of the new positivity statement.

value.rationale: CG and BFGS are canonical accelerated solvers, while nonnegative iterates matter whenever coordinates represent masses, rates, concentrations, or other positive quantities. The theorem gives a complete, dimension-free safety frontier and proves the earliest minimal-dimensional failure above it. Unlike a routine rate estimate, it answers a feasibility question not controlled by the usual energy-norm convergence theory, and the Broyden-family transfer shows the boundary applies across a major class of exact-line-search second-order approximations.
